interviewQuestions.question: How would you solve Word Search — given a 2D grid of letters, does a path of adjacent cells spell out a target word?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd treat the grid as a graph where each cell's neighbors are the up/down/left/right cells inside bounds, and run DFS with backtracking from every cell whose letter matches the word's first character.

The recursive function takes the current cell and how far into the word we've matched. Base case: matched the full word length, return true. Otherwise, if the coordinates are out of bounds or the cell's letter doesn't match the word's current character, return false immediately — that's the entire pruning mechanism.

The part I'd call out explicitly: cells can't be reused within one path, and rather than a separate visited set, I'd temporarily overwrite the cell with a sentinel character that can't match any letter, then restore it right before returning — whether the recursive calls succeeded or not. That mark-and-restore is the grid version of "choose, explore, unexplore."

Complexity is roughly O(rows × cols × 4^L) for a word of length L in the worst case, but in practice most starting cells die on the very first character check, so it's much faster than the bound suggests.

**Testing:** whether you can adapt the general backtracking template to a grid and handle the mark-and-restore pattern correctly.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Fundamentals

interviewQuestions.question: Why do you mutate the board in place instead of using a separate visited set for Word Search?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
It's a space trade-off with no correctness downside, as long as the sentinel value is safe to use. A separate `visited` set of coordinates costs O(word length) extra space on top of the recursion's own call stack — every recursive call would need to add and remove a coordinate. Overwriting the cell in place costs zero extra space, since it reuses memory the board already occupies.

The trick only works because the sentinel — typically `'#'` or any character outside the word's alphabet — is guaranteed to never match a real letter, so a later step in the same path checking that cell always sees a mismatch, exactly as if it were marked visited. I always restore the original character right before the function returns, regardless of whether the recursive calls found a match, because every sibling call further up the stack still needs to see the original board.

Where I'd switch back to a visited set: if the board's alphabet could plausibly include the sentinel character itself, or if the board needs to remain readable by concurrent code during the search — situations where mutating shared state isn't safe. For a single-threaded interview solution, in-place marking is the standard, expected answer.

**Testing:** whether you understand why the mark-and-restore trick is safe here specifically, not just that it's a common pattern.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Trade-offs

interviewQuestions.question: Now you need to find all matches for any word out of a list of thousands of words in the same grid. How does your approach change?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Running the single-word DFS once per word in the list works but re-explores the same shared prefixes over and over — if a thousand words start with "CAR", that prefix's grid paths get independently re-walked a thousand times.

The fix is building a **trie** from all target words first, then running one DFS pass over the grid guided by the trie instead of a single word string. At each cell, instead of comparing against a fixed `word[i]`, I check whether the trie node has a child matching the current letter — if not, that branch prunes immediately, and it prunes for *every* word sharing that now-dead prefix simultaneously, not just one.

When a trie node marks the end of a word, I record a match at that path (and can mark it so it isn't reported twice if two words share a suffix path). I'd also delete matched words from the trie as I find them to avoid revisiting completed paths, and prune trie nodes with no live children to keep the trie itself shrinking as words get found.

The complexity is still bounded per starting cell similarly to the single-word case, but a single grid traversal now answers all words at once instead of one traversal per word — a huge win when the word list is large and shares structure.

**Testing:** whether you can recognize when a shared-prefix data structure changes the complexity class of a repeated search, a very common senior-level extension of Word Search.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Scaling

interviewQuestions.question: Your Word Search implementation is correct on small test grids but crashes with an index error on a grid with an edge case you didn't test. What's the likely bug?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
My first check would be the order of the bounds check versus the character comparison in the DFS function. The correct order is: check `0 <= r < rows and 0 <= c < cols` **first**, and only index into `board[r][c]` after confirming that's true. If the character comparison runs first, any recursive call that steps one cell past an edge or corner raises an index error immediately — Python doesn't short-circuit an out-of-range access just because a bounds check would have caught it afterward.

This specific bug is sneaky because it can pass small test grids if the test happens not to probe every edge and corner, but it fails the moment the outer loop's start-cell search or the DFS itself reaches a boundary cell and tries a direction pointing off the grid — which happens on essentially any grid larger than 1x1 once enough starting cells and directions are tried.

To confirm, I'd add a boundary cell explicitly to a test case (start the search from a corner) and check the stack trace points at the indexing line, then verify the bounds check genuinely runs before that line in the code, not just textually above it but actually evaluated first due to short-circuit `and`/`or` ordering.

**Testing:** whether you can spot an ordering bug in boundary-check logic, a very common real bug class in grid-search code.
